excerpt: Qventus sells AI operational assistants that automate hospital work such as surgical scheduling and discharge planning. KKR led its $105 million Series D in 2025.
content:
Qventus makes AI software for hospital operations. Rather than supporting clinical decisions, its "AI teammates" take on operational work: filling operating room time and growing surgical volume, planning patient discharges early so beds free up, managing inpatient capacity and staffing, and coordinating the many handoffs inside a health system. Its website quotes Allina Health on gains in robotic and spine surgery volumes, and says health systems can co-develop new AI operational assistants with it through an AI Solution Factory.

In January 2025 Qventus announced a $105 million Series D led by KKR, made up of $85 million in equity and $20 million in venture debt, with Bessemer Venture Partners and new strategic investors including Northwestern Medicine, HonorHealth and Allina Health, Business Wire and Healthcare IT Today reported. The company said its technology was used by more than 115 hospitals and health systems and that it would use the money to bring AI assistants into more care settings, building on its Surgical Growth and Inpatient Capacity products. MedCity News covered the round as part of a wave of healthcare AI investment.

Qventus does not publish prices; hospitals contact its sales team. Its buyers are health systems in the United States, and it competes with operations tools from LeanTaaS and with capacity and scheduling features built into electronic health record systems.

We have not used Qventus for this page. It brings together Qventus's own website and the reporting linked under Sources, and says where each fact comes from. Nothing here is paid placement.
